title: Giselle Silva at '23 Points' in Career, Vows Powerful Finish for GS Caltex - 조선일보
content: Cuban star, nearing career's end, aims to repeat championship success with new teammate Tanacha Suksot “If I were to compare my volleyball career to a 25-point set, I’d say I’m at around 23 points.” Giselle Silva (35, Cuba), who led GS Caltex to last season’s championship and won both the V-League Regular Season Women’s Division MVP and Championship MVP, did not deny that her volleyball career has entered its final stretch. However, she emphasized that reaching “23 points” does not mean she will ease up as she approaches the end. Instead, she wants to pour all her strength and energy into securing the final points. “A professional athlete’s job is physical. If the time comes when I can no longer show the same power as before and must sit on the bench, I’ll step down. I want to finish my career while still demonstrating the same energy and power I have now. I must keep showing my relentless drive for victory until the end.” Silva is currently training in Hitachinaka City, Ibaraki Prefecture, Japan. When she met with reporters at the Astemo Rivale training facility for the Japanese women’s volleyball team on September 11, she expressed pride at being the first foreign player in the V-League to spend four seasons with a single team. For Silva, who has traveled across the world playing volleyball, GS Caltex is a special team. She never expected to stay this long when she first arrived in Korea. Like before, she could have moved to a new country after one season for another challenge. But after one season in Korea, her perspective changed. Rather than packing her bags again and starting from scratch in an unfamiliar country, she wanted to stay where both she and her family felt comfortable. Seeing her daughter Ciana (6) adapt well and enjoy life in Korea deepened her desire to remain. Last season, Silva displayed monstrous power by recording a success rate of over 50% (50.63%) after 200 attack attempts in the postseason, leading GS Caltex to a perfect 6-0 championship run. Despite chronic knee pain, she scored over 30 points in six consecutive games, delivering a valuable trophy to the team. However, she insisted the championship was not her individual achievement. “There were ups and downs, but we found solutions. I’m proud of my teammates who worked with me to overcome difficulties and achieve victory. They supported me a lot.” Her faith in the team remains unchanged ahead of the new season. When asked what gives her confidence in reclaiming the top spot, Silva did not hesitate. “It’s confidence. We did it last season. Why can’t we do it again this season? If every player on the court shares that confidence, I believe we can repeat the feat. Most importantly, my teammates have grown significantly. It’s visible.” This season, Silva has a formidable new teammate: Tanacha Suksot (26, Thailand), who faced her on the opposite side of the net in last season’s championship finals. Suksot, an outside hitter for the Thai national team who played for Korea Road Public Corporation last season, joined GS Caltex as an Asian Quota player this season. Silva recalled the intense rivalry with Suksot during the championship finals, where they exchanged fierce glances. When she first heard that her former opponent would become a teammate, Silva thought, “This will be fun.” “Tanacha is great at defense and has a fierce attack. Our chemistry will be good, and we’ll show fans exciting volleyball they’ll love.” Suksot also alleviates the offensive burden on Silva. When opponents focus on defending Silva, Suksot can open alternative attacking avenues, diversifying GS Caltex’s offense. The number most associated with Silva is “1,000.” She became the first V-League player to score over 1,000 points in three consecutive seasons. While it’s a remarkable record, it also reflects how heavily GS Caltex relied on her offense. “1,000 points? I don’t think it’s a perfect situation for the team if I’m the one scoring them. Still, this record holds personal pride. It’s a number built by enduring an entire season with strong physical and mental resilience.” GS Caltex head coach Lee Young-taek said, “It’s true Silva handles many attacks, but her efficiency is close to 50%, which is high. Maximizing high-probability attacks is the path to victory.” Another pillar supporting Silva’s career is her family. Balancing motherhood and her athletic career while moving across the globe is not easy. Her husband, Luis, made it possible. “My husband’s life changed 180 degrees. He prioritized my career over his own to let me continue playing. Without his sacrifice and support, I wouldn’t have lasted this long. I can focus entirely on volleyball on the court because of him.” Asked how she wants to be remembered by V-League fans, Silva answered without hesitation: “I want to be remembered as a player who never gave up and kept fighting until the end.”

title: Thanacha Sooksod joins GS Caltex to seek growth and lead younger players - CHOSUNBIZ - Chosunbiz
content: "I thought I needed to throw myself into a new environment to develop further.". She chose change instead of familiarity. Thanacha Sooksod (26), an outside hitter and former Thailand national team member, will take on a new challenge wearing the GS Caltex uniform. Thanacha, who first stepped into the V League in 2023 wearing the Korea Expressway Corporation (KEC) uniform, described her time there as "one of the best memories of my life." Although it was full of good memories, she did not want to be complacent. She judged that she needed to change her environment to grow one step further as a volleyball player. Met at GS Caltex's training camp in Japan on the 12th, Thanacha said, "I felt that a change of environment was necessary to develop one step further as a volleyball player. I thought that throwing myself into unfamiliar situations could be an opportunity to take one more step forward in life." The first club to reach out to Thanacha after she decided to change was GS Caltex. She explained the reason for her transfer, saying, "When I started considering a transfer, GS Caltex contacted me first," and "I wanted to go to a team that valued me highly." Coincidentally, it was a team she had faced as an opponent in last season's championship finals. From the opponent's court, GS Caltex was a team that, once it got a flow, was hard to stop. Thanacha recalled, "Once they got momentum, it was really difficult to break that flow. Especially, the 'chemistry' among the players looked very tight. You could feel that they trusted each other on the court." Now she has entered that closeness directly. There are also changes. Her position within the team. Born in 2000, Thanacha was a relatively young player at Korea Expressway Corporation (KEC), where many veterans were present. At GS Caltex, she has become someone who must lead younger teammates. She laughed, "At Road Corporation, during training when we divided into the older sister team and the younger sister team, I was like the eldest sister of the younger team. But here, I belong to the older sister side to the extent that I can't show any childishness." One of the things GS Caltex expects from Thanacha is balance in attack. Until last season, the team's attack was largely concentrated on Gyselle Silva. Silva boasted such powerful attacking ability that she became the first in V League history to surpass 1,000 points for three consecutive seasons. With Thanacha's addition, there is an expectation that Silva's attacking burden can be eased. But Thanacha shook her head at the phrase 'I must help Silva.' "Volleyball is a team sport. Other players must also participate in the attack for volleyball to be easier and more enjoyable. Rather than 'I must ease Silva's burden,' I think it's important for each player to fulfill their role." Silva also welcomed the arrival of the new teammate. After hearing that Thanacha was coming to GS Caltex, she expressed her expectations, saying, "She defends well and is a good attacker, so I think we can play fun volleyball together." Hearing Silva's words, Thanacha smiled brightly. "I'm really grateful she said that. It means a lot to me. Becoming a good player when we are together—that is the image of a volleyball player I want to be." The values Thanacha pursues are clear. She values being remembered as a "good teammate" as much as personal performance. She said, "You can't always play well while playing volleyball. There are days you perform well and days your skills don't show properly," adding, "But being a good teammate is something I can work on. When I look back on my volleyball life later, I hope I'm remembered as 'a good team member.'" So she thinks her role becomes more important the less the game goes as planned. She approaches teammates first and says, "It's okay. Let's try again," lifting the mood. That mindset also reflects the unique culture of Thai volleyball. Thanacha cited 'enjoying volleyball' as a characteristic of Thai volleyball. She said, "Thai players don't dwell too deeply on mistakes. They laugh together and quickly move on to the next play," adding, "I think approaching a game with that mindset lifts the atmosphere and improves performance." She also cited overcoming physical disadvantages with diverse attacks as an advantage of Thai volleyball. "Thai players are not generally very tall, so they use combinations a lot. They don't attack from only one spot but move inside and outside to add variety to the attack. I want to show that a lot this season." She is also proactive in building a 'good team' off the court. Liking board games is more than a simple hobby; it's one way to get closer to teammates. Thanacha explained, "If everyone just looks at their phones in free time, there is no time to look at each other's faces and talk," adding, "When we play board games, we naturally sit facing each other, talk, and get to know each other better. I think the intimacy and trust built off the court eventually show up on the court." Wearing a new uniform and standing at a new starting line, Thanacha's goal is clear: winning the championship. She tasted the joy of finishing first in the regular season with Korea Expressway Corporation (KEC) but did not reach the top of the championship final. She said emphatically, "I want to win while doing my best. I will never give up on that goal." Even while running toward the goal, she does not want to lose her own color. A player who chases the ball to the end and is the first to smile and reach out to teammates when the team wavers. That is the image Thanacha envisions of herself at GS Caltex. "I always want to be a teammate who gives good energy. This season, I'll try to smile a lot." We use cookies to enhance your experience and analyze traffic. title: Candidate aghast at $500Gs bill for 'field with fence' dog park - Toronto Sun
content: A candidate for council says he was told that spending half a million dollars to fence in a dog park is 'just the way it is' at Toronto City Hall See more Toronto Sun on Google — save as a Preferred Source How do you spend half a million dollars fencing in a field? Shawn Allen thinks City Hall has a spending problem, and his first, best example is the new off-leash dog park at Lawrence Ave. E and Starspray Blvd. – east of Port Union Rd.  He wants to be the next city councillor for Scarborough-Rouge Park, and for him the project has been something of a crash course in Toronto politics. “It’s a field with a fence. We’re paying for a fence. That’s what it is,” Allen told the Toronto Sun. “We’re paying to fence in a space – I think it’s 800 square metres, if I’m not mistaken – and we’re paying half a million dollars for that. And the majority of the cost is consulting fees, mobilization fees, arborists, geotechnical engineers, all these things. “Why do we need a geotechnical engineer to put a fence around grass? The dogs were running along the grass perfectly fine before they put up the dog park. Why can’t the dogs run along the grass and just fence it in?” Subscribe now to read the latest news in your city and across Canada. City Hall hasn’t provided an answer for the “why.” While the park was designed with input from residents in Scarborough-Rouge Park ward, the plan never went before committee to be scrutinized by city councillors and the public. The city wouldn’t confirm the project’s $500,000 price when asked by the Sun. The only official number comes from a motion by the incumbent councillor, Neethan Shan, to redirect $200,000 in funding for improvements from a nearby park, the Royal Rouge Tot Lot, to the off-leash area. Allen said he’s confident in the price because of a conversation with the project coordinator. “I said, why does it cost 500,000? She’s like, ha ha, that’s just the way it is. I go, what do you mean that’s just the way it is, ha-ha-ha? “We gotta figure this out. This city’s going broke.” In a statement, City Hall said construction at both the dog park and the Royal Rouge Tot Lot should be complete this fall. A final project cost and name for the dog park are still to come. Your noon-hour look at what's happening in Toronto and beyond. Please try again The city did not address questions about what the redirection of funds means for the Tot Lot, Allen’s conversation with the planning official or why a dog park would need a six-figure budget. Allen said he’s a dog owner and is in favour of off-leash parks – “but I’m just looking at the cost.” “For 500,000, you could house 108 people at $2,200 a month, so what’s the priority?” Shan redirected the Tot Lot funds with a member’s motion during May’s City Council meeting. While councillors can debate such motions, they typically draw little attention and this one passed with a quick show of hands. In an emailed statement, Shan focused less on the off-leash park and more on the Tot Lot improvements, which had a $300,000 budget – but got $530,000 in funding. Shan said he secured money from a playground enhancement program to pay for more amenities, including an accessible picnic table, a fitness pod and more play features. That funding allowed him to send the $200,000, from a pool of what’s known as Section 37 money, to the dog park budget. (While the Sun asked why a dog park would need a half-million-dollar budget, Shan did not address this in his statement.) “The kids didn’t get less money, they got more,” Shan wrote. “We listened to the community, improved the original plan and secured more investment to deliver more for residents.” Shan’s a rookie councillor but a veteran politician. He spent years as a school board trustee in both York Region and Toronto, then briefly served as city councillor for Scarborough-Rouge River, winning a 2017 byelection in what was Ward 42 in the city’s former 44-ward model. The ward map was redrawn, and he narrowly lost to Jennifer McKelvie in 2018’s election. When McKelvie left last year for Parliament, Shan won another byelection, while Allen placed third. The left-wing advocacy group Progress Toronto – founded by Mayor Olivia Chow’s political lieutenant Michal Hay – endorsed Shan last year, hailing him as a “progressive champion.” But Allen said constituents tell him that Shan is hard to get ahold of. He said City Hall is failing to provide Toronto with “value of service.” “The city is a corporation,” Allen said. “We have all these school board trustees as executives on the board of something that they’re not familiar with.” Allen was born and raised in Scarborough, and has run a mortgage brokerage for about two decades. Times are tight for many Torontonians, and Allen thinks City Hall isn’t helping. “We have food bank lines wrapped around the corner in West Hill. People are hungry,” he said. “People have mortgage arrears, people have tax arrears and the mayor’s committed to raising property taxes next year at the rate of inflation. Well, we’re still catching up from the 20% you raised it over the past three years, so now you’re going to put people behind the 8-ball even more … We can’t ask homeowners to find savings when the city’s not doing the same.” Postmedia is committed to maintaining a lively but civil forum for discussion. title: BMW F 450 GS Price Hike: Check New Variant-Wise Prices - motoroids.com
content: Months after launching the much-awaited F 450 GS, BMW Motorrad has revised the prices of the ADV in India. Introduced as the brand’s new entry point into the GS family, buyers will now have to spend up to ₹30,000 more depending on the variant. The price hike applies across all three versions, with no new features or mechanical updates included in this revision. The F 450 GS is manufactured in India through BMW Motorrad’s partnership with TVS Motor Company. It replaced the G 310 GS as the brand’s smallest GS adventure motorcycle in the country. The Base and Exclusive versions have received a ₹25,000 price hike, while the top-spec GS Trophy gets the highest increase of ₹30,000. All prices listed below are ex-showroom. The GS Trophy continues as the most expensive version and comes with extra equipment, including BMW’s ERC (Easy Ride Clutch) system. This technology reduces the need to operate the clutch manually during gear shifts. Each variant is offered with a single colour option. The Base and Exclusive variants come in Cosmic Black, while the GS Trophy features Racing Blue with red and white graphics. BMW has left the engine completely unchanged. The F 450 GS continues to be powered by a 420cc, liquid-cooled, parallel-twin engine that produces 47bhp and 43Nm of torque. It is paired with a six-speed gearbox and features a slipper clutch. The use of a twin-cylinder engine separates the F 450 GS from the older G 310 GS, which relied on a single-cylinder motor. The F 450 GS is built on a tubular steel frame. It features a 43mm KYB upside-down front fork and a KYB rear monoshock, offering 180mm of suspension travel at both ends. The motorcycle rides on a 19-inch front wheel and a 17-inch rear wheel with dual-purpose tyres. The motorcycle has a seat height of 845mm. It provides an upright riding position and built-in wind protection for riders planning longer journeys. A 6.5-inch TFT display comes standard, supporting smartphone connectivity and navigation functions. Road, Rain and Enduro riding modes are offered as standard. The higher variants add Enduro Pro mode and extra electronic equipment. Other features include heated grips and adjustable levers. While the GS Trophy benefits from the ERC system, cruise control is not offered on any variant. The BMW F 450 GS now starts at Rs 4.95 lakh and goes up to Rs 5.60 lakh. Nothing else has been added with the latest price revision, so the higher prices are the only change for buyers.

title: Thanacha Suksom Stresses Teamwork in New GS Caltex Role - 조선일보
content: Thai Star Balances Offense, Fosters Camaraderie After Transfer from Korea Expressway “I thought that to develop further, I needed to throw myself into a new environment.” Thanacha Suksom, 26 years old, an outside hitter from the Thai national team, chose a new challenge this season. After joining the Korea Expressway Corporation in 2023 and competing in the V-League, he described his time with the team as “one of the best memories of my life.” Still, he opted for change. Rather than staying in a familiar environment, he wanted to test himself in a new one. Meeting Thanacha at GS Caltex’s Japanese training camp on September 12, he said, “I felt that a change of environment was necessary to take my volleyball career to the next level. Throwing myself into unfamiliar situations could be an opportunity to move forward in life.” The first team to reach out was GS Caltex. “When I started considering a transfer, GS Caltex contacted me first,” he said. “I wanted to join a team that highly valued me.” Coincidentally, GS Caltex was the team he faced in last season’s championship finals. At the time, observing them from the opposing court, he found them a tough opponent with few weaknesses. “Once they gained momentum, it was really hard to break their flow. The ‘chemistry’ between the players seemed incredibly tight. I could feel their trust in each other even on the court.” The biggest change Thanacha feels now is being part of the “senior line.” Born in 2000, he was relatively young at Korea Expressway Corporation, where veterans were abundant. But at GS Caltex, he has become a leader responsible for guiding younger teammates. “At Korea Expressway, I was the oldest in the ‘younger group’ during training, but here, I’m firmly on the senior side—no room to act young,” he laughed. One role GS Caltex expects of Thanacha is balancing the team’s offense. He needs to share the burden that previously fell heavily on Gisele Silva, who led the team’s attacks last season. Silva became the first player in V-League history to score over 1,000 points in three consecutive seasons. However, Thanacha shook his head at the idea of “easing Silva’s burden.” “Volleyball is a team sport. When everyone participates in attacks, it becomes easier and more fun. Rather than ‘I must reduce Silva’s load,’ each player fulfilling their role is key.” Silva also welcomes the new teammate. Upon hearing of Thanacha’s joining, she said, “She works hard on defense and has good attacking skills. I think we can play fun volleyball together.” When relayed Silva’s words, Thanacha smiled and said, “I’m really grateful for those words. It means a lot to me. Becoming a better player together is exactly what I want as a volleyball athlete.” “You can’t always perform well in volleyball. There are days when things go smoothly and days when your skills don’t show. But being a good teammate is something I can strive for. When I look back on my volleyball career, I hope to be remembered as ‘a good teammate.’” That’s why Thanacha’s role becomes clearer when matches don’t go as planned. He is the first to approach a teammate and say, “It’s okay. Let’s try again.” This mindset also reflects Thai volleyball culture. Thanacha highlighted its biggest feature as “enjoying the game.” “Thai players don’t dwell too long on mistakes. They laugh and quickly move on to the next play. I believe this attitude keeps the atmosphere alive and improves performance.” Overcoming physical disadvantages with diverse attacks is another characteristic of Thai volleyball. “Since Thai players aren’t generally tall, we use a lot of combinations,” he said. “Instead of attacking from one spot, we move inside and outside to add variety. I want to showcase this style a lot this season.” Off the court, Thanacha also focuses on building a “good team.” His love for board games isn’t just a hobby—it’s a form of “teamwork training” to bond with teammates. “If everyone just stares at their phones during free time, there’s no chance to talk face-to-face. Board games make us sit together naturally, leading to conversations and deeper understanding. The closeness and trust built off the court eventually show on it,” he explained. Thanacha’s goal this season, in his new uniform, is obviously a championship. With Korea Expressway, he experienced the joy of finishing first in the regular league but didn’t reach the championship finals’ summit. “I want to do my best and win the championship. I won’t give up on that goal,” he said. Even in the pursuit of the title, he doesn’t want to lose his unique color. On the court, he chases the ball until the end, and when the team falters, he’s the first to smile and reach out to a teammate—this is how he envisions himself. “I want to be a teammate who always gives good energy. This season, I’ll smile a lot.”

title: What a Fed Rate Hike Could Mean for US Stocks - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. Investors are pricing in a higher likelihood that the Federal Reserve will hike rates after core CPI inflation rose in August more than economists had estimated. However, a rate hike may not keep the US stock market from climbing higher, says Jonathan Shugar, head of Cross Asset Sales in Goldman Sachs FICC and Equities, on The Markets podcast. Companies reported strong earnings growth in the second quarter, and valuations near the 10-year average are not stretched, he explains. Shugar also discusses why a Fed hike may not restrain investment in artificial intelligence, the risks in longer-term interest rates, and the potential opportunity for investors in consumer experience stocks. Chris Hussey: This is The Markets. I'm Chris Hussey, and today is Friday, September 11th. Before we start, I want to acknowledge that it's 25 years since the 9/11 attacks. As our chairman and CEO, David Solomon, said in remarks, "Our firm joins the community in honoring the lives lost that day, as well as the first responders, recovery workers, and survivors, and everyone who suffered from 9/11 related illnesses." I'm also joined today on the Goldman Sachs trading floor by John Shugar. John is head of cross-asset sales within FICC and Equities. John, thanks so much for joining us on The Markets. Jonathan Shugar: Thank you for having me, Chris. Great to be here. Chris Hussey: Well, first time, long time for you, I know. Tell us a little bit about cross-asset sales. That could encompass anything. What exactly is it? Jonathan Shugar: What we like to do is be like our clients, which is ultra-flexible as to where the opportunity set is. That's really what drives it. The team is about 25 people, specialists across equities, derivatives, execution, credit, rates, and FX. And so really what we're able to help people do is capture these inflection points in markets, whether that's going from a growth equity cycle to a credit cycle, or whether that is looking at asymmetric hedges. And you've seen the utility of that ever since the subprime crisis to different rate hiking cycles or credit protection, where we look for asymmetric hedges. And we'll talk a little bit more about that later on. Chris Hussey: Yeah. Well, it sounds like having the inflection guy here is perfect because we just got the CPI report. The FOMC meets next week. Looks like we might be in for an inflection. What do you make of the CPI report and the reaction that the market's had so far? Jonathan Shugar: So, I think that the market reaction is telling you that they're going to hike next week. We have something like 84% odds priced for that, and for 50 bps before year-end. That's not to say that inflation has not followed some of what the people who want to hold say, which is you haven't seen shelter inflation continue to go and goods inflation moderated. It was really driven by things like communication services. That being said, with it being so hot and the Fed having said they're data-dependent, the market is telling them that in some ways it's actually more dangerous not to hike because you might lose control of the back end in that case, and that's one of the bigger risks to the market. Chris Hussey: Yeah, it's a great point, cause the Fed controls the front end through their Fed funds rate, but the back end is controlled by the markets, and the markets can do anything they want there. Let's talk a little bit about equities for a second here, because this also is back to school week, and we've had a series of things that always happens in the back to school, and people come back and they're trading heavily. The market, though, has kind of flat-lined since early August. What do you make of the rally that we've had and where do you see it going from here? Jonathan Shugar: So we've had some near-term challenges. Momentum has had an extraordinarily tough last two months. When you look at technical levels here, you have both CTA and systematic flows against you in the near term. That being said, we just finished our Communacopia conference. One of the biggest themes in the market right now is AI. The companies coming out of there could not have been more bullish. And to the people who say the market is expensive, we're trading at a 19 PE. That's the 10-year average. We've had S&P earnings growth of something like 30% on the second quarter. So, if you look at that, you basically have a market where all of the heavy lifting has actually been done on the earnings side. And when you think about the drivers going forward, there's terrific opportunities within various AI consumer sectors which are off highs, to really say that, well, over the next few weeks we may have a lot more speed bumps. But if you and I are sitting here at year-end or we're sitting here next year, we're talking about an S&P that's probably well over 8,000. Chris Hussey: Okay, John, let's examine de-globalization because your customers can invest anywhere in anything all at once, and there have been a lot of geopolitical risks. We're seeing it in the oil tape. What are your customers saying about those geopolitical risks today? Jonathan Shugar: So, one of the most interesting things has been the things that really impacted the market negatively when you think about Liberation Day as the original tariff announcement. Those have become less relevant to price action as we go forward, and it's a trend that we've really seen since COVID, which is the duration of opportunity to take advantage of dislocations to the market is getting less and less, and the moves to correct to the upside are much more violent. Now, when you think about geopolitical risk out there, there's certainly things which are near term. You mentioned oil. If you look at Brent right now, you're trading around 104, but you look out one year, you're buying Brent at, with a seven handle on it. So, this is still viewed as a more near-term problem. That doesn't mean you can't have local disruptions. On the product side, whether it's gasoline, diesel, heating oil, probably looks incrementally worse for Europe than the US, but that can certainly be something that comes up. All of that should be relatively short duration in terms of impact but can certainly drive local price action. When we think more broadly, there are geopolitical impacts on both the positive and negative side. Obviously there's a good reason why you might want to look at a country like Brazil, and we've seen investors increasingly look to buy upside there as they're going into an election in October. Chris Hussey: Brazil. When the market zigs, you zag. I love it. Okay. You're a risk guy. Let's talk a little bit more broadly about risks here because I know you have a view. What are the risks out there that you're watching and how do you wanna hedge them? Jonathan Shugar: So, as we think about what the largest risk on the board is, it really, outside of some of the true tells, which are global geopolitical risk exploding is really in the back end of the rate curve. And that is because, one, there's natural impulse for this to be higher. You have global fiscal deficits. This is not just a US problem. This is everywhere. You have a ton of AI issuance, so hyperscalers doing about $800 billion of CapEx this year. Our analysts estimate something around $1.2 trillion next year. So, there's a lot of natural supply which is competing for money. Now, if you get a really sharp move in rates, cause equities can tolerate higher rates. It's really just the pace of change that has the biggest impact. So, the way we like to hedge that is really in two ways: either buying outright payers or payer spreads on the back end, the 30-year part of the swap curve, or looking out and doing something like a CMS cap, which is the shape of the curve between front and back end, and we think that there's good returns out there. Now, we always love 10 X-type trades. On reasonable strikes, you can probably still make five to six X your premium. And so that's what we're talking to investors about now. Chris Hussey: Five to six X. I thought everything was 10X, but okay. You say equities can tolerate higher rates, but do they tolerate higher rates because as long as the rates are going higher because of inflation, equities are indexed to inflation, so they're a nominal asset, so they go up? What happens if the higher rates are tied to something more like a debasement trade? Jonathan Shugar: So, if they're tied to a true tail risk debasement trade, that would obviously be negative in the short term for equities. If you get true hyperinflation, and you can go back to Zimbabwe or anything you want, that could be really good for equities because they are a nominal asset. That being said, I think the reason people are thinking about all of this is, one, economic growth remains good. The fact is that hiking25 or 50 basis points doesn't change the need for the strongest balance sheet companies in the world to be investing heavily in CapEx, given how transformative a technology AI is going to be, and the consumer outside of the low end still is okay. And so, you compare that to the fact that most consumer stocks are trading 30% plus off their 52-week highs. There just seems a real disconnect here. And so, as you think about equities going forward, people got very surprised by things like biotech performing so well. And biotech, another thing that typically has a lot of correlation negatively to higher end rates being higher. Well, I think consumer and there are pockets of that we like, there are pockets of that we don't like, could be the thing that surprises into your end. By the way, another plug for our conferences, we've got our consumer conference next week. So, we're going to know a lot more after that. Chris Hussey: Okay, you gave us a great hedge trade, but give us one more. What's the trade? Jonathan Shugar: So, I think that there's a lot that can be done here. Number one, within consumer, there's both longs and things that we're more cautious on. On the long side, the experiential type names, whether it's cruise, whether it's events, things that people really want to do and spend money on, especially at the high end, that continues to see a lot of growth. On the flip side, there have been companies releasing agents for consumers. Well, guess what? If you don't have to spend two hours to switch your phone plan to a cheaper plan that's probably something that could be really impactful, and so we're a little bit more cautious on some of the impacts there. We mentioned AI briefly. A lot of the CapEx picks and shovels are trading well below market multiples. A lot of the semis type names trading well below market multiples. You're seeing capital return in some of those places and other interesting things. We think this is a temporary air pocket and those have good runway ahead of them. Chris Hussey: Terrific. Sum us up for this here. What are you watching for next week and the weeks ahead that we should be keeping our eyes on? Jonathan Shugar: So clearly watching the Fed next week, I think that's something where the press conference is going to be a lot more impactful than the actual if they do hike, hike. If they don't hike, that's actually very interesting and may have impact of its own. Outside of that, I think that any clarification on kind of the big picture questions from corporates as you go through the rest of the year on the efficacy of AI in terms of increasing revenue will get people really, really excited again. Outside of that, watching the Giants on Sunday. Hoping that's not another tough season to be a Giants fan. Chris Hussey: J-E-T-S, Jets, Jets, Jets. John Shugar, you're a wealth of information. Thanks so much for joining us. Chris Hussey: That does it for this week's episode of The Markets. I'm Chris Hussey. Thanks for listening. title: “One of the Biggest Statements So Far”: Skatta on Karol G’s “BbY WOW” Global Success - Kaboom Magazine
content: Our latest digital magazine is available for download - CLICK HERE >> “BbY WOW,” which samples the iconic “Coolie Dance Riddim,” gives the classic beat another major global moment. “This beat was different,” Burrell reflects on its enduring impact For years, music producer and industry figure Skatta Burrell has continued to reap the success of his iconic juggling, the Coolie Dance Riddim, as the 2003 production continues to find new life across international music. The compilation, listed by Rolling Stone among the 25 Riddims That Shaped Jamaican Music, became one of dancehall’s biggest international crossovers, powering hits including Elephant Man’s “Jook Gal,” Mr. Vegas’ “Pull Up,” Bounty Killer’s “Yuh Gwan” and more. Its reach stretched even further through Pitbull’s Latin smash “Culo” and Nina Sky’s Billboard Hot 100 Top 10 hit “Move Ya Body,” which was later remixed featuring Vybz Kartel. “The experience of witnessing multiple samples and remixes of the Coolie Dance Riddim is something I’ve been witnessing almost yearly since its release in 2003,” Burrell said, reflecting on the riddim’s longevity. More than two decades later, Coolie Dance continues to move beyond dancehall floors and into the global mainstream. Beyoncé moved to its pulse during her 2023 Renaissance World Tour, while Kehlani sampled the riddim on her 2024 viral hit “After Hours.” Its latest major moment comes through Colombian superstar Karol G, alongside Spanish artistes Judeline and rusowsky, whose “BbY WOW” samples the riddim and climbed to No. 1 on both the Billboard Global 200 and Billboard Global Excl. U.S. charts. The song generated 42.3 million global streams from August 28 to September 3 and has surpassed 116 million streams on Spotify. “This ‘BbY WOW’ hit is by far one of the biggest statements so far, and especially being a Spanish-language song, it seems to be captivating the world due to its infectious melodies and the dynamics and groove from the Coolie Dance beat,” Burrell shared. “No words can explain the gratitude and reassurance I get just knowing I created music that is definitely timeless.” Latin superstar Karol G gives the classic beat another major global moment. For Burrell, the riddim’s continued global success also validates the creative instincts behind a beat that sounded different from much of what surrounded it at the time. “I’ve always known this beat was different and out of the norm, and it reminds me that trying to fit in is never the way to achieving greatness,” he said. “What matters most is the way music makes you feel, and its main purpose is to evoke emotions and movement.” While Burrell admits he never predicted just how far Coolie Dance would travel, he always believed there was more to come from the production. “This global impact was never forecasted. However, I’ve always had that confident assurance inside that there’s always more to come from this Coolie Dance Riddim,” he added.
